notes.meaning: Ezekiel looks up and sees what looks like a throne of blue sapphire above the heads of the cherubim. This matches the glorious throne of God he saw earlier by the river Kebar. The Lord sits high above all heavenly creatures, showing that He is completely in control of the judgments about to fall.

The Lord commands the man dressed in linen to go under the cherubim, gather burning coals from among the wheels, and scatter them over Jerusalem. Earlier this same man marked faithful people for mercy, but now he is sent to carry out judgment. The scattering of fire shows that the polluted city will soon be burned and destroyed.

When the man in linen steps inside, the cherubim are standing on the south side of the temple, and a thick cloud fills the inner courtyard. A cloud often showed God's holy presence, but here it also shows His anger over the worship of idols in His temple. The angels stand ready, completely united in carrying out God's sentence.

The bright glory of the Lord rises from the cherubim and moves to the doorway of the temple. The temple interior is darkened by the cloud while the courtyard shines brightly with God's glory. God takes His first steps away from His home, showing that He will not dwell where sin is welcomed.

The sound of the wings of the cherubim echoes all the way out into the temple's outer courtyard, roaring like the thunderous voice of God Almighty. This immense sound shows that the heavenly creatures are in motion and ready to depart. It serves as a loud warning that massive changes are coming to Jerusalem.

The man dressed in linen obeys the Lord's command and enters among the whirling wheels, taking his stand beside a wheel. He does not hesitate to follow God's orders. God's messengers move with quick obedience to prepare the fire of judgment.

One of the cherubim reaches out a hand, picks up burning coals from the fire between them, and puts them into the hands of the man in linen. The man takes the coals and steps outside to scatter them across the city. This action shows that heaven's angels fully support God's holy judgment against Jerusalem's sins.

Ezekiel notices that the cherubim have the form of human hands under their wings. These hands explain how the cherub could pick up the burning coals and hand them to the messenger. They show that heavenly beings have skill and readiness to perform God's work.

Ezekiel sees four gleaming wheels, with one wheel standing beside each of the four cherubim. The wheels sparkle with the color of a precious beryl stone. These wheels represent God's active providence—His constant care and control over every turning event on earth.

All four wheels look exactly alike, appearing like one wheel set inside another at right angles. This unique design lets them roll in any direction without having to turn around. Even when world events look tangled and confusing, God's plans move with perfect order.

The wheels move directly toward any of the four directions without pivoting or turning aside. They follow wherever the leading cherub faces, rolling straight ahead. God's purposes never swerve or get distracted, but go directly to their goal.

The entire bodies of the cherubim, along with their wings, hands, and the rims of the wheels, are covered with eyes. This shows that God sees everything and governs the world with total awareness. While the city leaders falsely claimed the Lord could not see them, these eyes prove that nothing is hidden from God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase describing the bodies covered with eyes is missing in the ancient Greek translation (Septuagint) and may represent an early explanatory note added to the text.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel hears a loud voice call out to the wheels, naming them the whirling wheels. This call summons the entire wheelwork into rapid, whirlwind-like motion. Everything in creation responds immediately when God gives the command.

Each cherub has four faces: the face of a cherub, a human, a lion, and an eagle. In Ezekiel's earlier vision, the first face was called an ox, which suggests the face of a cherub had an ox-like appearance. These four faces represent strength, intelligence, boldness, and swiftness in serving God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Textual scholars note that this verse is absent from the early Greek Old Testament, and several modern translations render the face of a cherub as an ox to match Ezekiel 1:10.

notes.meaning: The cherubim lift themselves up, and Ezekiel recognizes them as the very same living creatures he saw earlier by the river Kebar in Babylon. This second vision reassures the prophet that the Lord is the same God everywhere. The same holy Lord who met the exiles in Babylon is now dealing with the rebellious city of Jerusalem.

Whenever the cherubim move, the wheels move right along with them, and when they spread their wings to rise, the wheels do not leave their side. The wheels never wander away or act on their own. God's angelic servants and the events of the world work together in complete harmony.

When the cherubim stand still, the wheels stop, and when the cherubim rise, the wheels rise with them. They move as one because the living spirit that directs the cherubim is also in the wheels. God's Spirit guides all created things so they fulfill His holy purposes.

The glory of the Lord leaves the temple threshold and rests above the waiting cherubim. The people in Jerusalem assumed God would never leave His temple, but their persistent sin has driven His presence away. God leaves step by step, showing how reluctant He is to depart from His people.

The cherubim lift their wings and rise from the ground with the wheels beside them, stopping at the eastern gate of the Lord's house. The glory of the God of Israel hovers above them at this temple exit. God pauses once more on His way out, giving the people one last chance to repent before His glory departs completely.

Ezekiel confirms that these were the living creatures he saw beneath the God of Israel by the river Kebar, and he knows for certain they are cherubim. As a priest, he knew the gold cherub statues inside the temple, but now he sees the real, living angels. This confirmation assures him that God's revelation is true and trustworthy.

Each cherub has four faces, four wings, and the form of human hands beneath its wings. Ezekiel repeats these exact details so his readers know the vision was real. God gave this clear repetition so a stubborn people could not dismiss the prophet's message.

The faces of the cherubim look identical to the ones Ezekiel saw by the river Kebar, and each creature moves straight forward. They never wander from their path as they carry out the Lord's commands. God's plans move ahead with steady focus, and nothing on earth can turn them aside.
